newsitem.title: UK: FX IN EUROPE -DLR AND STG GAIN GROUND AFTER ROUT.
newsitem.headline: FX IN EUROPE -DLR AND STG GAIN GROUND AFTER ROUT.

text.p: The dollar and sterling regained poise after a sell-off on Friday but a sluggish tone in U.S. asset markets clipped their wings as traders awaited the Bundesbank's repo tender on Tuesday and key data later in the week.
Dealers said some players stepped back into the market as buyers after getting caught short dollars and pounds on heavy profit-taking last Friday.
"They got stopped out today when some big buyers came in to pick up the dollar at lower levels," said a senior trader at a German bank in London.

The dollar's health has not been damaged by Friday's drop of about four pfennigs and four yen as the broad-based picture remain dollar-positive as U.S. econonomic fundamentals outshine those of Germany and Japan, analysts said.

"The current phase in dollar/mark could simply come to resemble the consolidation which occurred before the dollar blasted through the 1.80 and 1.85 regions before," said Michael Lewis, international economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

A recovery in the mark/yen cross from two-year lows boosted dollar/yen but the pair ran into resistance at 116.30/40. Dealers said the dollar was well bid by Japanese importers, possibly because of a sell-off in the Nikkei 225 stock index, which suffered a loss of almost four percent.

The summer holiday period has reduced the number of players active in the market and exaggerated movements. During Friday's sell-off four big players - two Swiss and two U.S. banks - dominated trading, dealers said.

At 1517 GMT the dollar was at 1.8555/65, up from 1.8470/80 at the European close on Friday and from a low of 1.8383 on Friday. Dollar/yen was at 115.87/95, up from 114.84/89 late Friday and its trough at 114.25. Mark/yen was at 62.42/45 from 62.76/78 and off its two-year low below 62.

The sharp decline of the dollar last week was in part triggered by simmering speculation that the Bundesbank might switch to a variable rate repo or nudge the rate higher from 3.00 percent at present at Tuesday's repo tender.
But many analysts expect the Bundesbank to stay put because a rise in interest rates would hurt the nascent economic recovery in Germany.

The sell-off accelerated late in Europe on Friday after Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing was quoted in a newspaper as saying German price developments were moving in the wrong direction in all areas, including consumer prices.
Earlier last week - when dollar/mark was trading around 1.89 marks - Issing had said the Bundesbank was worried about dollar/mark's rapid rise.

Some analyst say, however, that there is a small chance of a "double-decker repo", which could take the form of a two-week fixed repo at the current rate of 3.00 percent as well as a variable repo for a longer dated tranche. "Only unless the Bundesbank fails to stabilise the mark below 1.90 is this policy response expected to be taken in an attempt to shore up the mark's defenses, something we see as unlikely," said Lewis. "We continue to look for an unchanged repo policy this week."

The fate of U.S. asset markets after Friday's sharp sell-off is likely to give the dollar near-term direction, traders said. The Treasury market remained sluggish on Monday and stocks were weaker in choppy trade.
Later this week, the focus will be on U.S. data, with July retail sales and producer price data on Wednesday, followed by CPI figures on Thursday. German CPI data are also out this week.

Sterling firmed after last week's rout which started when markets started taking the view that UK interest rates have peaked for now. Cable was up despite the firmer dollar. The pound was at 2.9578/88 from 2.9272/77 late on Friday. Cable was at $1.5935/45 from $1.5852/62. Sterling hit a low at 2.9143 on Friday.
UK July PPI data caused little reaction as they were largely in line with expectations even though analysts noted some pressure on output prices.
The next focus for sterling will be retail price data on Tuesday and employment, earnings figures and the Bank of England's quarterly inflation report on Wednesday
